title: TrailGenic Heat Training Thermoregulation Dataset
description: Shell dataset module for TrailGenic physiology adaptation science modeling thermoregulatory adaptation from repeated exercise in hot environments.

records.mechanism: Heat acts as the dominant environmental cardiac-cost driver after adaptation control

stimulus.comparison_context: hot chaparral sessions versus cool alpine sessions

physiological_response: Average heart rate increased by approximately 0.11 bpm per °F after controlling for adaptation.
Hot chaparral routes produced elevated load and lower Day-2 HRV compared with cool alpine efforts.
Thermal exposure remained a stronger acute cardiac-cost driver than altitude once adaptation state was considered.
adaptation_outcomes: Heat becomes a primary progression variable for load management.
Cool alpine routes can produce higher recovery quality despite greater altitude and elevation gain.
Thermoregulatory cost should be separated from terrain and altitude cost in future modeling.

supporting_science.finding: Heat stress increases thermoregulatory and cardiovascular strain during exercise.
Heat adaptation improves physiological tolerance but does not eliminate the cardiac cost of thermal load.

records.mechanism: Heat acclimation through repeated endurance exposure

supporting_science.finding: Heat acclimation improves thermoregulatory control and cardiovascular stability during exercise in hot environments.
Heat adaptation improves sweating efficiency and reduces physiological strain during exercise.

records.mechanism: Cardiovascular adaptations to repeated heat stress

stimulus.exercise_type: repeated endurance sessions in warm environments

physiological_response: reduced heart rate at submaximal workloads
adaptation_outcomes: reduced heart rate drift in warm environments

supporting_science.finding: Heat acclimation improves cardiovascular function and endurance performance.
